title: DPIIT startup recognition in 2026: eligibility, benefits, how to apply
excerpt: The 2026 Startup India rules: who qualifies for DPIIT recognition, the section 140 (old 80-IAC) tax holiday, angel tax status and how to apply on NSWS.

content:
DPIIT recognition is the government certificate that makes an Indian company, LLP, partnership or cooperative an official "startup" under the Startup India programme. Since February 2026 you qualify if you are up to 10 years old (20 for deep tech), have had turnover below ₹200 crore (₹300 crore for deep tech) in every year so far, and are working on innovation; you apply free on the National Single Window System (NSWS), and the certificate typically arrives within two working days.

The rules changed this year. A new notification dated 4 February 2026 replaced the 2019 definition, doubled the turnover ceiling and created a deep tech category, and the government recognised a record 55,200 startups in 2025-26. Meanwhile the old section 80-IAC tax holiday now lives in section 140 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, and the angel tax has been abolished. This guide covers eligibility, benefits, the tax position and the application, step by step. It is general information, not legal or tax advice; confirm details with a chartered accountant or company secretary and the official portals linked below. (₹1 crore is ₹1,00,00,000.)

Key takeaways

  • Eligible entities: private limited companies, LLPs, registered partnerships and cooperative societies, up to 10 years from incorporation (20 for deep tech).
  • Turnover must have stayed below ₹200 crore in every past financial year, or ₹300 crore for deep tech startups.
  • The three-year 100% profit deduction (old 80-IAC, now section 140) is narrower: only companies and LLPs incorporated from 1 April 2016 and before 1 April 2030, with turnover up to ₹100 crore and a separate board certificate.
  • Angel tax (section 56(2)(viib)) does not apply from assessment year 2025-26 and is absent from the 2025 Act; older years can still be scrutinised.
  • Recognition is free on NSWS; DPIIT says it has appointed no agents.

What changed in 2026

The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) issued a new startup definition on 4 February 2026, G.S.R. 108(E), which supersedes the 2019 notification, according to Treelife. The main changes:

Criterion2019 definition2026 definition
Turnover ceiling₹100 crore₹200 crore (₹300 crore for deep tech)
Age limit10 years10 years (20 years for deep tech)
Deep tech categoryNoneNew, attribute-based definition
Cooperative societiesNot eligibleMulti-state and state/UT cooperatives eligible
False information-Express power to revoke recognition

A deep tech startup is one building solutions on new scientific or engineering knowledge, with high research and development spending relative to its size, significant new intellectual property with a plan to commercialise it, and substantial technical uncertainty, according to Treelife's reading of the notification. Law firm Nishith Desai Associates adds that the restrictions on investing in assets such as residential property, luxury goods and speculative holdings apply for as long as a company holds recognition, according to Nishith Desai Associates.

Demand is at a record. DPIIT recognised more than 55,200 startups in 2025-26, up 51.6% from about 36,400 the year before, taking the total to about 2.23 lakh by 31 March 2026, according to Inc42, citing the commerce ministry. Recognised startups report more than 23.36 lakh direct jobs, and nearly 48% have at least one woman director or partner.

Who is eligible

The Startup India portal lists five conditions, according to Startup India:

  1. The entity is a private limited company, or registered as a partnership firm, LLP or cooperative society. Sole proprietorships are not on the list.
  2. Turnover has been below ₹200 crore (₹300 crore for deep tech) in each previous financial year.
  3. It is no more than 10 years old (20 for deep tech), counted from incorporation or registration.
  4. It works towards innovation, or improving existing products, services or processes, and can create jobs or wealth.
  5. It was not formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business.

Recognition lasts only while all conditions hold. Crossing the age or turnover limit ends startup status for the purposes of the notification.

The benefits, in plain terms

Regulatory relief

  • Self-certification. Recognised startups can self-certify compliance with six labour laws, with no inspections for five years, and with three environmental laws for "white category" industries, which face only random checks, according to Startup India.
  • Patents. Fast-tracked examination, an 80% rebate on patent filing fees, and facilitator fees paid by the government.
  • Public procurement. Exemption from earnest money deposits, and for manufacturing startups, from prior-experience and prior-turnover criteria in government tenders.
  • Faster exit. Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, eligible startups can be wound up within 90 days of applying.

Money

  • Seed Fund Scheme. The Startup India Seed Fund Scheme has an outlay of ₹945 crore, channelled through incubators: grants of up to ₹20 lakh for proof of concept or prototypes, and up to ₹50 lakh through convertible debentures or debt-linked instruments for market entry. Applicants must be DPIIT-recognised and incorporated no more than two years before applying, according to the government's India Science and Technology portal.
  • Credit guarantees. The Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups, re-notified on 8 May 2025, covers up to ₹20 crore per borrower: 85% of the amount in default for loans up to ₹10 crore and 75% above that. The annual fee is 2%, 1.5% for startups from the north-east or led by women, and 1% in 27 "champion sectors", according to TaxGuru. Lenders include banks, eligible NBFCs and SEBI-registered alternative investment funds (AIFs).
  • Fund of Funds 2.0. The Budget for 2025-26 announced a new fund of funds with a fresh ₹10,000 crore, noting that AIFs backed by the first fund had received commitments of more than ₹91,000 crore, according to the Budget speech. Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 launched on 13 April 2026, with SIDBI as implementing agency and a focus on deep tech, early-growth funds and innovative manufacturing, according to MediaNama. The government invests in venture funds, which then invest in startups; you do not apply to it directly.

The tax holiday: section 80-IAC becomes section 140

The best-known benefit is a 100% deduction of profits from the eligible business for any three consecutive years out of the first ten. From 1 April 2026 it sits in section 140 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, which largely carries over section 80-IAC. Its conditions, according to an analysis on TaxGuru by chartered accountant Ruchi Chawla:

  • Only companies and LLPs qualify, not partnerships or cooperatives.
  • Incorporation between 1 April 2016 and 31 March 2030. The Budget for 2025-26 extended the window by five years to startups incorporated before 1 April 2030, according to the Budget speech.
  • Turnover not above ₹100 crore.
  • A certificate from the Inter-Ministerial Board (IMB).

Note the mismatch: recognition now allows turnover up to ₹200 crore, but the tax holiday still stops at ₹100 crore. A recognised startup can therefore lose the deduction while keeping its other benefits.

The IMB is convened by a joint secretary of DPIIT, with members from the Department of Biotechnology and the Department of Science and Technology, usually meets about once a month and processes cases in order, according to Startup India's FAQs. Under the revised process, complete applications are reviewed within 120 days. Approvals are selective: DPIIT cleared 187 startups across two meetings in spring 2025, taking the total to more than 3,700 since the scheme began, according to The Tribune. Against about 2.23 lakh recognised startups, that is under 2%.

The holiday only helps once you make a profit, so choose your three years for when profits are expected.

Angel tax: where things stand

Section 56(2)(viib), the so-called angel tax, taxed share premiums above fair value as income. In her July 2024 Budget speech the Finance Minister proposed to abolish it "for all classes of investors", according to the speech. The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 made the provision inapplicable on or after 1 April 2025, that is from assessment year 2025-26, and the Income-tax Act, 2025 has no equivalent, according to a June 2026 TaxGuru analysis by CA Sundram Gupta.

Two caveats from the same analysis. First, assessments for assessment year 2024-25 and earlier remain open, so share issues from 2023-24 or before can still draw notices. Second, sections 68 and 69 on unexplained credits and investments still apply, so you must be able to show who your investors are and where their money came from. The Startup India portal still links to a "Section 56 exemption" application, which matters mainly for those older years.

Abolition removes a reason founders sought recognition, and recognised startups keep other funding tools, such as the statutory convertible note explained in our SAFE notes and iSAFE explainer describes.

How to apply, step by step

  1. Incorporate or register as a private limited company, LLP, partnership or cooperative, and keep your incorporation or registration certificate ready.
  2. Prepare a short description of how the business innovates or improves a product, service or process, and how it can create jobs or wealth. The FAQs say this and the certificate are the core requirements, according to Startup India.
  3. Create an account on nsws.gov.in. On the dashboard, choose "Add Approvals", then "Central Approvals", find "Registration as a Startup" and add it, according to Startup India.
  4. Fill and submit the form using the company's own email and mobile number. There is no fee, and DPIIT says it has not appointed any agency, representative or franchise to apply on your behalf.
  5. Download the certificate. It is usually issued within two working days of a complete application as a system-generated, verifiable certificate.
  6. Apply for the tax holiday separately through the Startup India portal if you are a company or LLP that qualifies, and track the IMB meeting notices.
  7. Apply for schemes such as the Seed Fund Scheme through an incubator, and tell lenders you are recognised when seeking loans under the credit guarantee scheme.

Bottom line

Recognition is free, quick and now open to larger and older companies, so most eligible founders should get it for the compliance relief, patent rebates, procurement access and funding schemes. Treat the tax holiday as a separate, selective application that is worth it only for companies or LLPs heading into profit under ₹100 crore of turnover. With angel tax gone, the main tax risk is now proving the source of investor money. For who is raising and from whom, see our funding tracker.

FAQ

Is DPIIT recognition mandatory for a startup?

No. It is optional, but it is required to use Startup India benefits such as self-certification, patent rebates and the tax holiday.

How long does DPIIT recognition take?

The certificate is typically issued within two working days of a complete application on NSWS.

Can a sole proprietorship get DPIIT recognition?

No. Eligible forms are private limited companies, LLPs, registered partnerships and cooperative societies.

What is the new section number for 80-IAC?

Section 140 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026.

Is angel tax still applicable in 2026?

No, it does not apply from assessment year 2025-26, though earlier years can still be reassessed.

Does DPIIT recognition cost anything?

No. The commerce ministry charges no fee and has appointed no agents.
